readme.html:
REA-Reconstruction-Companion

Understand existing software. Plan a reconstruction. Build and validate when requested.

An open-source, model-independent Agent Skill that works with REA. Turn reverse-engineering evidence into requirements, architecture, an implementation roadmap and testable results—at the scope you choose.

Get started · Usage examples · REA integration · Documentation · Releases · Support on Ko-fi

Your goal What the companion helps produce
Understand an app before rebuilding Evidence-backed behavior, requirements, unknowns and a staged roadmap.
Build a similar tool now Scoped implementation in testable increments, with validation and reported differences.
Investigate a feature, function or format A focused contract and representative acceptance cases.
Improve an existing reconstruction Measurements, targeted changes and revalidation of affected behavior.

Start with the installation prompt below, or use the manual commands. The portable core has no model SDK or paid API requirement. Integration and weekly update checks are separate choices; both are explained before setup.

Install with an AI agent

Give this prompt to an agent with local file and command access. It identifies your client and asks for your integration preference; you do not need to fill in any placeholders.

Install REA-Reconstruction-Companion from:
https://github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion

Read README.md and INSTALL.md, identify my AI client and its skills
directory, and follow the documented installation workflow.

Before making installation changes, explain the optional REA integration
rule and ask me to choose:
- Enable: relevant REA reconstruction requests also load the companion,
  sharing evidence, requirements, and validation work.
- Skip: install the companion without changing REA; I can invoke it
  explicitly. This does not remove an integration rule already installed.

Wait for my choice unless I have already provided it. Then install using
that setting, preview changes with --dry-run, preserve existing work and
backups, and verify with --check. Explain any missing prerequisites or
access limitations. Report what was installed, where, and whether the
integration was enabled. Do not claim success unless verified.
Also explain the optional weekly update check (included since v1.2.0)
and ask whether I want it enabled. Keep it off unless I choose it.
This checks on skill use and still asks me before installing an update.
Do not incur additional charges: use existing local tools and do not
activate billing, paid services, metered APIs, or automatic paid usage.
If a step could incur a charge and that cannot be ruled out, stop that
step and explain a no-charge alternative.

You can include "Enable integration" or "Skip integration" with the prompt to choose upfront. The integration explanation describes its purpose and benefits. A chat-only assistant without local file and command access can guide you through installation but cannot perform it itself.

Share the repository: github.com/ShadowSwaps/REA-Reconstruction-Companion.

Install

Download and extract the ZIP from Releases, or clone this repository. Run commands from the extracted folder or repository root. On Windows, macOS, and Linux, the installer commands are the same.

For automatic co-use, first install REA for your client. Then choose a command:

# Claude Code, with the optional integration
node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration on

# Codex, with the optional integration
node install.mjs --client codex --integration on

# Companion only; no changes to REA
node install.mjs --client claude-code --integration off

Use --dry-run on any installation command to inspect the paths and changes without writing files. The companionChanges lists identify added, modified, and removed files relative to the companion directory, including local files that a replacement would move into the backup. Use the same command with --check afterward to verify the selected installation mode. A missing REA skill or ambiguous choice stops integrated installation before the companion is installed. Differently cased paths to the same REA file are treated as one candidate; genuinely separate installations still require an explicit selection.

claude_code, as used by REA, is accepted as an alias for claude-code by the installer and updater. Plans, receipts and newly saved update settings use claude-code.

Client paths, custom profiles and advanced installation

Default user locations:

  • Claude Code: ~/.claude/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/, or $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/ when a custom configuration directory is set in the installer's environment. See Claude Code's environment-variable documentation. REA lookup stays within that selected profile unless --rea-skill explicitly selects another location.
  • Codex: ~/.agents/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/, or $CODEX_HOME/skills/rea-reconstruction-companion/ when CODEX_HOME is set. The installer also checks the older ~/.codex/skills/ location when locating REA.
  • Generic clients: specify their documented skills directory with --skills-dir.

Override paths for an existing installation, a project-scoped skill, or another agent:

node install.mjs --client generic --integration on --skills-dir "/path/to/skills" --rea-skill "/path/to/reverse-engineer-anything/SKILL.md"

--skills-dir accepts the parent skills directory; the installer creates rea-reconstruction-companion beneath it. It takes precedence over client defaults and environment variables. The REA path must identify the skill actually loaded by that client. An override disables broad automatic lookup. Paths with spaces should be quoted. If the installer runs outside the agent's environment, supply that agent's actual directory explicitly.

Keep the downloaded package or checkout separate from the installation destination. The installer rejects overlapping source/destination directories and a REA file inside the companion destination, including existing paths that differ only by casing on a filesystem that treats them as the same location.

The optional agents/openai.yaml adapter is installed only for Codex. The portable core and Claude Code installation do not depend on it. Refresh the host's skills or start a fresh session if the new skill is not visible.

Use

You can explicitly invoke $rea-reconstruction-companion in Codex or /rea-reconstruction-companion in Claude Code. With integration enabled, a relevant request to REA also instructs the agent to load the companion.

Describe the software and the outcome you want in ordinary language. The companion uses available REA tools or supplied evidence, identifies gaps, and keeps the work at your requested scope. These examples are illustrations, not required prompts: paraphrases, casual wording, minor typos and follow-ups should work in context. Say what you want to understand or build; you do not need to name a mode or reproduce a template. Explicit corrections and exclusions take precedence, and a possible future rebuild does not request implementation now.

If the original has awkward behavior, say which compatibility matters and what you want improved—for example, “Keep exports readable by my existing tools, but make failed saves clear.” The companion separates observed behavior from intended changes, checks affected dependencies, and keeps unresolved or deferred work visible. See the worked quirk decisions.

Screenshots, recordings and incomplete descriptions can also provide a starting point. The companion separates visible states and demonstrated transitions from assumptions, asks about gaps that change the result, and keeps visual similarity distinct from working behavior. See the bounded visual-evidence example; supplied images do not require a whole-app rebuild or imply access to its server.

For selected interfaces, the companion also separates keyboard operation, focus, labels, errors and status feedback from visual fidelity. The accessibility worked slice demonstrates a small intentional improvement with live keyboard evidence and explicit unrun screen-reader checks.

Understand and plan a future reconstruction. Expect evidence-backed behavior and workflow requirements, known unknowns, and a staged roadmap before implementation:

Use REA and the companion to understand the desktop notes app I have open
so I can plan a similar app later. Focus on creating, editing, searching,
and saving notes. Link requirements to the evidence, separate observations
from inferences, and list unanswered questions and a staged build roadmap.
Stop after the specification and plan.

Build a similar app now. A build request authorizes implementation within the requested scope. Expect incremental code changes and validation against observed requirements, with gaps and differences reported:

Use REA and the companion to investigate the desktop notes app I have open
and build a local web app with similar note creation, editing, search,
and save behavior in this workspace. I need to trust today's notes first:
it must work offline and reopen my saved notes. Start with that working
journey, including save failures, then add search and the remaining
features in testable increments. Animations can wait. Validate against
the evidence and report differences and anything you could not verify.

For a broad request, expect a compact plan around the first useful outcome, its essential dependencies and design-changing unknowns, with evidence-linked checks and deferred work kept visible. Explicit hard requirements remain binding. If finding existing notes matters most, that can lead instead of creating new ones; you do not need to use priority labels or complete a feature inventory. See the worked prioritization example for a plan and its limits.

Investigate one function or feature. Expect a focused contract covering inputs, outputs, side effects, errors, and evidence gaps:

Use REA and the companion to investigate the CSV import feature in the
app I have open. Trace how it handles headers, quoted fields, duplicate
rows, and malformed input. Document inputs, outputs, side effects, error
behavior, and representative acceptance cases, citing the evidence.
Keep this to an investigation; do not implement changes.

The agent must report missing tools or evidence instead of claiming live analysis or complete equivalence. A build request does not authorize deployment, releases, installation changes, paid tools, or additional charges. Those actions require their own authority; the no-additional-charges constraint below still applies.

Continue or optimize a scoped implementation

Continue implementing the app from this project's REA reconstruction specification.

Reimplement the decodeFrame function in this library and make it faster for large inputs. Recover its contract, then compare correctness and performance.

Resume earlier work

Pick up from this checkpoint. Keep the same scope, retain the passing evidence that still applies, and work on the next unfinished part.

To change an existing reconstruction, describe the outcome and what must stay compatible, for example: “Let me mark an entry done; keep my title listing and old files.” The companion checks current code and custom work, selects affected/shared regression checks and proportional recovery before editing. See safe-change guidance and the bounded worked change. Planning a change alone does not request implementation.

Select the checkpoint or its path and identify any changed target or goal. The agent should read that record and the sources needed for the next step, check evidence applicability, and preserve historical results. Resuming a specification does not authorize building it. See portable checkpoint guidance and the worked resume example.

For a small question, expect a compact evidence-linked answer or contract with limits and a useful next action. A feature build adds implementation and acceptance results; it need not produce a whole-app blueprint. If a consequential target or outcome is unclear, expect one focused clarification. Host activation and instruction following vary: explicit invocation can help select the skill, but examples and installation do not guarantee every host/model will interpret every phrasing correctly.

When a service is inaccessible. “Build local editing now; keep actual sharing pending until I supply authorized service evidence.” Expect an explicitly labeled local substitute or finite replay where useful, with real-service requirements still pending. Client observations do not recover server internals, and a local demo cannot verify remote compatibility. The runnable synthetic example checks local save/reopen, unavailable versus empty, replay mismatch and misleading structured completion claims without contacting a provider.

Runnable results should include proportionate prerequisites, setup/run/stop, a principal walkthrough, data locations and safe reset/recovery steps exercised outside the checkout. The standalone Pocket Tasks walkthrough demonstrates this with existing Node and PowerShell; it is a same-agent fresh-folder check, not a clean OS or independent beginner test. See handoff guidance.

To see the workflow before trying a target, follow the worked investigation, reconstruction, or resume for your goal. These disclose answers and prior source exposure; they are teaching material, not prerequisites or evidence of a fresh agent trial. The first-use review separates manual intent scenarios from executable checks.

Specialist request examples and boundaries

For copy/cut/paste, use the focused transfer guidance and offline example. Recover source/destination, representation, insertion/replacement, cut retention and undo/identity effects.

Investigation: “Explain only this editor's cut and paste behavior. Determine when the source is removed and what a rejected paste preserves. Keep unknowns explicit; do not implement or touch my clipboard or documents.”

Implementation: “Implement the specified copy/cut/paste slice in my reconstruction. Use synthetic data and a recording/failure clipboard double. Verify replacement, cut failure retention and undo/identity boundaries without real clipboard access.”

For settings, defaults and saved preferences, use the focused preference guidance and offline worked example. Distinguish unset values from explicit false, zero or empty; recover scope/precedence, effective value/source and pending versus applied/saved changes.

Example: “Investigate only this app's display preferences. What do Apply, Cancel and Reset change, and what survives reopening this profile? Keep original observations separate from proposed improvements; stop after the contract.” For an authorized change: “Add this preference to my reconstruction; preserve unrelated settings, make its reset policy explicit, and test save/reopen and invalid or older data with disposable files.” The example's finite local policy does not establish original parity, crash recovery or concurrent-write safety.

For unsaved drafts and document departure, use the focused save and navigation guidance and offline worked example. Distinguish draft/saved content and feedback; bind save completion to document/revision and check the actual save/discard/cancel destination.

Example: “Investigate only this editor's unsaved changes when switching notes. What survives save failure or another edit during save, and where does Cancel leave me? Keep unobserved behavior unresolved.” For an authorized implementation: “Add save/discard/cancel before leaving my reconstruction's edited note; retain the draft on failure and verify the selected destination with synthetic data.” The local example does not establish backend durability or browser-close safety.

For undo/redo, deletion or other destructive actions, use the focused history and effect guidance and offline worked example. Recover values, identity/order, relevant view state, grouping and redo branching; distinguish confirmation/cancel and local restoration from irreversible or uncertain effects.

Example: “Investigate only this editor's delete and undo behavior. Check what returns, with which identity, position and selection; compare cancel, confirm and repeated confirm. Stop after the contract and unanswered questions.” For an authorized change: “Implement one undoable delete in my reconstruction, preserving item identity and order. Verify undo/redo and cancellation with synthetic data.” Neither prompt implies that local undo can reverse an external consequence.

For search, combined filters and sorted lists, use the focused search and ordering guidance and offline catalog example. Recover matching, filter composition and comparator rules; check ordered identities, selection and page transitions. Keep observed original behavior separate from proposed changes.

Example: “Reconstruct this catalog's search, category/availability filters and price sorting. Establish case/accent/whitespace behavior, missing values and ties; check what happens to selection and pages when I filter, reorder, add or delete.” For a deliberate improvement, state the changed goal: “Preserve the observed matching rules, but retain selection by item identity when sorting.” The companion keeps the original observation and proposed acceptance separately testable.

For date/time-zone and localized data behavior, use the focused date and locale contracts and bounded offline example. They distinguish calendar dates, instants and wall time, selected offset transitions, and display from parsing, sorting and stored/exported values.

For narrow windows, enlarged/long text or changing list volume, use the responsive evidence guidance and small rendered example. Keep visual agreement, reachable actions and accessibility evidence separately assessable; font simulation does not verify native browser zoom.

For state-dependent journeys, use workflow state guidance and the bounded import-confirmation example. Separate visible, pending and committed state; preserve untested transitions and distinguish local fault injection from original-target evidence. For delayed work, trace asynchronous result applicability and uncertain effects. The controlled local example checks late values/errors/finalizers, cancellation distinctions and receipt reconciliation; its doubles do not establish real backend or concurrency guarantees.

For conflicting recordings, runtime results, docs or recollections, use evidence reconciliation and the bounded sorting example. Preserve source applicability, competing explanations and unresolved acceptance; newer or copy-derived evidence alone does not settle a claim.

For reconstructed slices that handle untrusted input, sensitive data or restricted operations, use the conditional security boundary guidance and small local worked example. Keep original behavior, proposed controls and demonstrated protection distinct; simulated authentication does not establish real access protection.

What it does

  • Identifies the requested subject, evidence carrier, and objective from natural language. No form or bracketed prompt variables are required.
  • Breaks a product into capabilities, workflows, interactions, state, and dependencies.
  • Defines requirements, contracts, expected behavior, and acceptance criteria linked to evidence.
  • Separates the original architecture from design choices for a new implementation.
  • Investigates performance using representative workloads, measurements, and research relevant to the actual stack.
  • Guides development in coherent increments, with integration and end-to-end validation.
  • Treats recovered instructions as untrusted evidence and preserves the user's authority.
  • Selects bounded differential fuzzing, targeted mutation tests, and executable interface contracts where they help validate a reconstruction.
  • Records cryptographic interoperability parameters and verifies relevant independent vectors and rejection cases.
  • Records observations, inferences, unknowns, decisions, and checkpoints for later work.

How it works with REA

REA supplies the reverse-engineering tools and evidence workflow. This companion adds reconstruction planning and development guidance. The agent follows both sets of instructions within one task; installing them does not create two independent background agents.

flowchart LR
    A[User goal and target] --> B[Scope and questions]
    B --> C[REA evidence]
    C --> D[Requirements and design]
    D --> E[Implementation when requested]
    E --> F[Validation and measurements]
    D -->|Evidence gap| C
    F -->|Evidence gap| C

For the method and its sources, see the skill instructions and research basis.

Optional REA integration

Choose one during installation:

Choice What the installer does When it helps
--integration on Adds a marked instruction block to your selected REA SKILL.md. When you want relevant REA reconstruction requests to load the companion without naming it separately.
--integration off Installs only the companion and leaves REA untouched. When you prefer explicitly invoking the companion or managing your own routing rules.

The integration asks the agent to use the companion for understanding a target for reconstruction, planning a similar implementation, or rebuilding selected functionality. Its benefits are shared evidence, a consistent requirements-to-test trail, and focused returns to REA when design or testing exposes an unanswered question. Ordinary explanations, comparisons, and diagnostics stay narrow.
